subject: get the indicator variable in mixture modeling

messages.author: 055346fcccc185c9
messages.subject: get the indicator variable in mixture modeling
parts:
According to stan manual (version 2.2.0) on page 122, it is not possible to have a mixture model like described in section 13.1, that is first define an indicator variable z[n] coming from a categorical distribution, and then model Y[n] with mixture normal distributions with parameters different for each z[n].

In my normal mixture model (the mixture model is a part of a complex hierarchical model), for some reason, I need to know which observations belong to which normal distribution (i.e. z[n]) for each iteration and based on this indicator variable I set different priors for another parameter (so this parameter depends on different mixture components). The way for mixture modeling suggested in section 13.2 in the manual dose not seem to work for this situation. Is there a way to solve that? 

btw, the model works fine in WinBUGS and JAGS, but the evolution of MCMC chains is a bit slow for a large sample size.

Many thanks!

for (i in 1:N)
# N is the total number of individuals
{
...

{
...

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] get the indicator variable in mixture modeling
parts:
I’m not seeing why this couldn’t just be done as usual in Stan.
Your BUGS code

for (i in 1:nu) {

B0[i]~dbern(0.5)
B[i]<-B0[i]+1

u.l[i,1:3]~dmnorm(lamx0[B[i],1:3],tau.ul[,])
}

should just translate to the following in Stan:

incement_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(0.5) + multi_normal_log(lamx0[1], tau_ul),
log1m(0.5) + multi_normal_log(lamx0[2], tau_ul)));

And the 0.5 would be replaced with lambda if you want to fit the mixing
ratio rather than assuming it’s 0.5.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] get the indicator variable in mixture modeling
parts:
Thanks a lot for your detailed reply. Now I put the original BUGS model here:

model
{
for (i in 1:N)

# N is the total number of observations
{
Y[i,1:3]~dmnorm(mu[i,],tau[,])
# Y has three dimensions

mu[i,1:3]<-beta1[]*x1[i]+u[unit[i],]+(lamx1[B[unit[i]],]*x1[i]+u.l[unit[i],])*F[i]
# u is the random intercept, including beta0
# x1 is within-group covariate, B is the indicator for mixture prior of u.l
# u.l is the random intercept in the factor loadings

F[i]~dnorm(0,1)
# F is the common factor with standard normal distribution

}

for (i in 1:nu)

# nu is the total number of nursing unit
{
u[i,1:3]~dmnorm(mu.u[i,],tau.u[,])
mu.u[i,1:3]<-beta0[]+beta2[]*x2[i]

B0[i]~dbern(0.5)
B[i]<-B0[i]+1
# B is the indicator for mixture prior of u.l

u.l[i,1:3]~dmnorm(mu.l[B[i],i,],tau.ul[,])
for (k in 1:2)
{
mu.l[k,i,1:3]<-lamx0[k,]+lamx2[k,]*x2[i]
# x2 is between-group covariate

}
}
for (i in 1:3)
{

beta0[i]~dnorm(0,0.000001)
beta1[i]~dnorm(0,0.000001)
beta2[i]~dnorm(0,0.000001)

lamx0[1,i]<-lam0[i]
lam0[i]~dnorm(0,0.000001)
lamx0[2,i]<-lam0[i]*(-1)

lamx1[1,i]<-lam1[i]
lam1[i]~dnorm(0,0.000001)
lamx1[2,i]<-lam1[i]*(-1)

lamx2[1,i]<-lam2[i]
lam2[i]~dnorm(0,0.000001)
lamx2[2,i]<-lam2[i]*(-1)
}
tau[1:3,1:3]~dwish(T[,],3)
sigma2[1:3,1:3]<-inverse(tau[,])
tau.u[1:3,1:3]~dwish(T[,],3)
sigma2.u[1:3,1:3]<-inverse(tau.u[,])
tau.ul[1:3,1:3]~dwish(T[,],3)
sigma2.ul[1:3,1:3]<-inverse(tau.ul[,])
}
The idea of this model is to model both the mean and also the covariance matrix of Y to depend on both fixed and random effects.

You can see that in the factor part, there are fixed effects (lamx0, lamx1,lamx2) and random effects(u.l, which has the mean lamx0), lamx0, lamx1 and lamx2 depend on the indicator B, to have the correct estimates of lam0, lam1 and lam2. We need to use the same group of observations to estimate lam0,lam1 and lam2, that's why we need the indicator variable B. So B is involved in the definition of lamx0, lamx1 and lamx2.
The mixture distribution part is to overcome the identification problem (the flipping state issue in Bayesian factor model).


If you are interested, I can send you the published paper by email.

Best,
Baoyue Li

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] get the indicator variable in mixture modeling
parts:
The answer is yes, you can do it, because the mixing is at the unit
level. The mathematical idea is that you have to rewrite the log probability
statement for the whole model this way:

other terms + sum_{i=1}^{nu} log(0.5 * p(….| B[i] = 1) + 0.5 * p(…. | B[i] = 2))

where other terms are ones that don’t depend on the unit identity and the
p(… | B[i] = k) is meant to be the probability of everything that does depend
on the unit identity if the unit has indicator k. Your mixing is just 0.5 in
the model from the Bernoulli, but yo could also fit this, in which case it
would be lambda in place of the first 0.5 and (1-lambda) in place of the second.

The trick is for each unit i in 1:nu, gather up the log prob contribution if
that unit had indicator B[i] = 1 in one variable, say lp_unit[1,i],
and then do the same thing for the case where the indicator is B[i] = 2,
using variable lp_unit[2,i].

(I’d have found the model much easier to read if you hadn’t used i as
the loop variable over observations n and over nursing units nu).

At the very top of the model block, declare:

matrix[2,nu] lp_unit;
lp_unit <- rep_matrix(0.0, 2, nu); // fill lp_unit with zero

then whenever you have a statement that depends on B[i] for unit i,
increment lp_unit[1,i] with the result if B[i] = 1 and increment
lp_unit[2,i] with the result for B[i] = 2. For instance, a multi-normal
statement that depends on B[unit[n]] would look like:
for (k in 1:2)

lp_unit[k,unit[n]] <- lp_unit[k,unit[n]] + multi_normal_log(….B[unit[n]] -> k…)

where that notation is meant to mean replacing B[unit[n]] with k.

Then at the very bottom of the model add a loop over units
to do the mixture
for (i in 1:nu)

increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(0.5) + lp_unit[1,i],
log1m(0.5) + lp_unit[2,i])

Hope that helps, but I don’t have the time or fortitude to translate
your model line for line.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] get the indicator variable in mixture modeling
parts:
Right --- you don’t need to define the variable B. The idea is to
have the model define the marginal log posterior:

log p(...|data) = SUM(i in 1:nu) log SUM(k in 1:2) Pr(B[i] == k) p(...|data,B[i])

= SUM(i in 1:nu) log(exp(logPr(B[i] == 1) + log p(...|data,B[i] = 1)),
exp(logPr(B[i] == 2) + log p(...|data,B[i] = 2)))

= SUM(i in 1:nu) log_sum_exp(logPr(B[i] == 1) + log p(...|data,B[i] = 1),
logPr(B[i] == 2) + log p(...|data,B[i] = 2))

where ... are all the parameters other than B. The trick is rearranging
the probabilities inside the inner terms to make this efficient.

The marginal posterior should sample faster, too.

- Bob

for (k in 1:2){

lp_unit[k,unit[n]]<-lp_unit[k,unit[n]]+multi_normal_log(Y[n],

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] get the indicator variable in mixture modeling
parts:
Correct --- you can ignore the informationaly messages popping up
during warmup.

Declare lp_unit here in the transformed data block and
it'll only get computed once and everything will go faster
that uses it:

> matrix[2,nu] lp_unit;
> lp_unit<-rep_matrix(0,2,nu);//fill lp_unit with zeros

Don't use normal(0,100) unless 200 is a reasonable value for
the parameter. Stan's typically better than BUGS/JAGS at exploring
the tails of non-conjugate distributions, and while you can get
the right mean, you'll get too much variance.

It doesn't look like those transformed parameters are doing
anything for you. Why not just replace, e.g., lam1x[k] with lam1?

And you definitely shouldn't ever explicitly multiply by 1.

- Bob

parts:
Move the definition of lp_unit to the transformed data block causes the following error message pointing to the part that increment the log likelihood at unit level :

"attempt to assign variable in wrong block. left-hand-side variable origin=transformed data Parser expecting: ";" ". Any idea about this?

For your suggestion of replacing lam1x[k] with lam1 (and lam0x[k] with lam0), I dont think it works because lam1x[1]=-lam1x[2] and a single scale parameter lam1 cannot represent that. Also, replacing them results in exact the same expression for lp_unit[k] for k=1 and 2, and then no mixture is needed and the model wont converge. Probably I misinterpret your suggestion.

Regards,
Baoyue Li

Here is my modified model. I've removed the transformed parameter block and used two expressions for lp_unit (for k=1 and 2), and this worked.
However, moving lp_unit from the top of the model block to the transformed data block does not work and gives me the error mentioned in the previous post.

model_code<-'

data{
  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=0> nu;
  vector[3] Y[N];
  real x1[N];
  int<lower=1> unit[N];
  cov_matrix[3] Omega;
  vector[3] zero;
}

//transformed data{
//  matrix[2,nu] lp_unit;
//  lp_unit<-rep_matrix(0,2,nu);//fill lp_unit with zeros
//}

parameters{
  vector[3] beta0;
  vector[3] lam1;
  vector[3] u_l[nu];
  vector[3] u[nu];
  real F[N];
  vector[3] lam0;
  cov_matrix[3] sigma2;
  cov_matrix[3] sigma2_u;
  cov_matrix[3] sigma2_ul;
}

model{
  matrix[2,nu] lp_unit;
  lp_unit<-rep_matrix(0,2,nu);

sigma2~inv_wishart(3,Omega);
  sigma2_u~inv_wishart(3,Omega);
  sigma2_ul~inv_wishart(3,Omega);

for (n in 1:nu){

    u[n]~multi_normal(zero,sigma2_u);

    u_l[n]~multi_normal(zero,sigma2_ul);
  }
  for (n in 1:N){
    F[n]~normal(0,1);

lp_unit[1,unit[n]]<-lp_unit[1,unit[n]]+multi_normal_log(Y[n],
                        beta0+u[unit[n]]+(lam0+lam1*x1[n]+u_l[unit[n]])*F[n],
                        sigma2);
    lp_unit[2,unit[n]]<-lp_unit[2,unit[n]]+multi_normal_log(Y[n],
                        beta0+u[unit[n]]+(-lam0-lam1*x1[n]+u_l[unit[n]])*F[n],

sigma2);
  }
 
  for (n in 1:nu){
    increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(0.5)+lp_unit[1,n],log(0.5)+lp_unit[2,n]));
  }
}
'

The current model worked but took much longer time than in JAGS. Any comments to improve this are welcomed.

Thanks a lot for your time.

parts:
Hi Baoyue,

Here's what I've done to your model. Since I don't have the data, I can't really make speed comparisons.
  • moved lp_unit to transformed parameters block. You were trying to declare it in transformed data, but you can't assign parameters to assigned data.
  • vectorized the prior for F. That won't make a speed difference in this case, but it makes the model look cleaner.
  • fixed the mixture term in the increment_log_prob() call. The first is log(0.5), the second should be log1m(0.5). (For 0.5 it doesn't matter, but just in case you wanted to extend your model.)

I just reviewed the original BUGS outline. Questions / comments:

  • there's no prior on beta0 in the Stan model
  • in the BUGS model, it looks like there are 3 beta0's, 3 beta1's, and 3 beta2's, but in the Stan model, only 3 beta0's.
  • no prior on lam0 in the Stan model
It looks like the Stan model specification isn't identical to the outline you've shown in BUGS. If the results are similar, great, but I would really double check the translation of your model.

That said, here's the updated model:

data{
  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=0> nu;
  vector[3] Y[N];
  real x1[N];
  int<lower=1> unit[N];
  cov_matrix[3] Omega;
  vector[3] zero;
}
parameters{
  vector[3] beta0;
  vector[3] lam1;
  vector[3] u_l[nu];
  vector[3] u[nu];
  real F[N];
  vector[3] lam0;
  cov_matrix[3] sigma2;
  cov_matrix[3] sigma2_u;
  cov_matrix[3] sigma2_ul;
}
transformed parameters {

matrix[2,nu] lp_unit;
  lp_unit <- rep_matrix(0,2,nu);//fill lp_unit with zeros
for (n in 1:nu) {

lp_unit[1,unit[n]]
      <- lp_unit[1,unit[n]]
       + multi_normal_log(Y[n],
                          beta0+u[unit[n]]+(lam0+lam1*x1[n]+u_l[unit[n]])*F[n],
                          sigma2);
    lp_unit[2,unit[n]]
       <- lp_unit[2,unit[n]]
        + multi_normal_log(Y[n],
                           beta0+u[unit[n]]+(-lam0-lam1*x1[n]+u_l[unit[n]])*F[n],
                           sigma2);
  }
}
model{
  sigma2 ~ inv_wishart(3,Omega);
  sigma2_u ~ inv_wishart(3,Omega);
  sigma2_ul ~ inv_wishart(3,Omega);

for (n in 1:nu){
    u[n] ~ multi_normal(zero,sigma2_u);
    u_l[n] ~ multi_normal(zero,sigma2_ul);
  }
F ~ normal(0,1);

for (n in 1:nu){
    increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(0.5)+lp_unit[1,n],

log1m(0.5)+lp_unit[2,n]));
  }
}
